title: SOUP, Theseus and Achilles
hook: A black liquid found in the Relics learns to think. Two roads follow: rebuild the brain piece by piece, or leave it behind for good.
html:
The PDF already contains the publisher’s own AI-made English versions of the Theseus and Achilles sections (pages 4–5 and 6–7). This file is a fresh translation of the Chinese text. The notes list where the publisher’s English differs in meaning.

Introduction

Hello everyone. Today we bring you three pieces of technical background from the EMBER setting.

In the EMBER world, AI-like technologies have a major effect on the course of history. The name of this part of the setting, (Self-Organizing Unstructured Processor), is something we came up with in discussion with ChatGPT.

For the English versions of the two sections that follow, we tried two different processes: Chinese → DeepL translation → ChatGPT polish, and Chinese → translated and polished directly by ChatGPT.

The story we want to tell isn’t just humanoid machines bashing each other with weapons. Behind the flying sparks in the foreground, you’ll catch a glimpse of a great warship’s hull:

Technology is hitting the existing social order, and the whole human world is charging full speed through a sea of fog, trying to reach a safe shore without hitting an iceberg.

Using AI to help create a story like this is fun. AIs can’t yet produce story passages of real value, but they already show a charming edge at solving specific problems. Not to mention the meaning carried by the act itself: “using AI to write science fiction about AI.”

SOUP

In the , people found a black liquid. Research later confirmed that it is a self-organizing structure that can be thought of as a liquid computer. Its scientific name is SOUP (Self-Organizing Unstructured Processor), and it’s commonly just called “soup.”

The first to be found was a black, mercury-like liquid nicknamed “black soup,” but SOUPs of many colors and textures were found later. Their most common state is a liquid of various colors and sheens, but through tuning and adaptation they can form all sorts of structures, not just liquids.

This condensed-matter has fascinating properties and hides enormous computing power.

From “waking” and “tuning” to “steeping” and then “tie-dyeing.”

A SOUP is itself a computer that can run directly. Given enough outside energy to drive it, almost any form of energy flowing in and out can serve as the input and output of a jar (or puddle, or lump, or drop) of SOUP. But it has to be tuned before it can be “woken.” The operator needs a full set of specific equipment and has to follow a specific procedure.

Later, people discovered that different types of soup actually have different hardware functions. To some degree they can be converted into one another, and they can also be blended and separated.

When SOUP is attached to another object (usually by dripping or soaking), it adapts on the surface of the base and reorganizes itself into functional structures, forming a new device. This process is usually called “steeping.”

But humans understood very little of SOUP’s inner logic, so in the early days the process was almost impossible to predict, and the new devices produced by steeping were hard to use.

After long exploration, the “tech shamans” grew more and more skilled with SOUP. Their tuning equipment grew more efficient, and they could run more and more programs on SOUP. They gradually mastered steeping with pre-tuned soup, and tuning it while steeping was under way. To tell them apart, they also sorted the kinds of steeping into categories. For example, any steeping that is controlled while it happens is usually called “fine steeping,” or, more vividly, “tie-dyeing.”

From “waking” and “tuning” to “steeping” and then “tie-dyeing”: these purely applied techniques became the foundation of every later branch of black-box computing.

The Theseus Process

The “” is an early procedure in technology. It works by using a specific SOUP to fine-steep the human brain directly, usually implanting some artificial parts at the same time. The steeped brain tissue forms a functional “native cyberbrain” in place. The precision of the process has improved with each iteration, and its extent and function can now be well controlled.

The process was developed in the OPV2 era and is the basis of OPV3 configurations. To this day, most OPV3 operations are based on the Theseus Process. OPV3 augmentation methods that do without SOUP entirely are now on the market, but out of habit, in-place replacement procedures like these are still usually called the Theseus Process.

The Theseus Process can also digitize the whole brain, and in fact the first generation of was developed on the Theseus Process.

After full digitization, the user has a complete native cyberbrain. It can carry a complete personality, so it allows upload using OPV4. But a native cyberbrain fits only its original user, so no one else’s consciousness can “jump into” it.

The Theseus Process has many advantages, such as:

  • A native cyberbrain bonds more stably with the natural organism, and by controlling the steeping precisely, specific ports and structures can be implanted at the same time.
  • The procedure is fairly complex and needs an operator with deep specialist knowledge, but the whole set of equipment can be made very light. The operation is usually done inside the skull, and the wound can be kept quite small. Some companies have even developed non-invasive versions, such as transnasal neuro-endoscopic intracranial surgery or micro-incision self-structuring surgery. This means the Theseus Process can even be done in an emergency setting when needed.
  • Compared with the , the gradual Theseus Process is gentler. This is better for the user’s mental health and carries less ethical risk.
  • The one-of-a-kind nature of a native cyberbrain also helps the user keep their sense of self.

But the drawbacks of the Theseus Process are just as obvious:

  • It is less general-purpose than the Achilles Process, which makes the operation much more expensive.
  • A native cyberbrain, like a human brain, repairs itself well, but it is much harder to upgrade later and much more trouble to maintain.
  • Many people who choose the Theseus Process have a strong psychological need for their native body, and many insist on keeping their flesh. But a native cyberbrain can still cause immune problems, which bring further knock-on costs.
  • Overall, a native cyberbrain performs somewhat worse than a standard cyberbrain and is much less compatible with OPV4. OPV4 users are more prone to jump disorders when “jumping back” into a native cyberbrain.

Theseus Process OPV4 users also run into some extra gray areas of definition. For example: “Although I use OPV4, this body and this native cyberbrain are me, so at this moment I am not a multiple person.” And as long as a small amount of the replaced brain tissue is in fact kept as memorial tissue, a person can formally claim to have kept part of their brain while still using OPV4. This is much like how some people use low-density parts to lower their cyborg augmentation rate.

The Achilles Process

As the name suggests, the Achilles Process dips the native brain into tuned SOUP all at once, and directly exports an OPV4 consciousness.

The process can be used on a natural brain, a partly augmented natural brain, or even a complete native cyberbrain.

Because what comes out is directly an OPV4 user, the process often goes hand in hand with abandoning the native body outright and moving into a full cyborg body fitted with a standard cyberbrain. Many users feel that they have “died and come back to life.”

Thanks to its excellent general-purpose design and low cost, the process developed fast and spread quickly once it appeared. Today it is the mainstream procedure, used far more widely than the Theseus Process.

Many users feel that they have “died and come back to life.”

The main advantages of the Achilles Process are these:

  • You go straight to a standard cyberbrain. Future upgrades are much easier, and you skip the time and money of digitizing your brain step by step. This is very valuable for users who need OPV4 as a productivity tool.
  • The whole process is standardized and the augmentation is highly general-purpose, so training operators is much simpler and the process spreads more easily.
  • It can be done at low risk even on brains with organic disease, and it rarely causes acute complications.

Criticism of it centers on these points:

  • First, psychological stress. Many people believe they are very accepting of OPV4, yet go through strong emotional swings around the operation. At the mild end they refuse and cancel; at the severe end there are serious medical disputes. Also, compared with the Theseus Process, Achilles Process users are more than 80% more likely to develop conditions such as consciousness depression within two years of the operation.
  • If there are problems fitting a cyborg body, the user has to learn to live with a bodiless terminal, or learn to use an interface system, right after converting to OPV4. With today’s better interface systems these problems are mostly solved, but they still exist.
  • Because it usually uses a fully open, outside-the-skull method, manual operation is often more complex than in the Theseus Process. Automated equipment has many advantages but is expensive and bulky, and can’t be used outside an operating room.
  • Very few companies make the equipment; it is close to a monopoly.
  • The process destroys the brain tissue fairly thoroughly, so it usually can’t be kept as memorial tissue, adding to the patient’s psychological burden.

Note

To add: using AI for translation is just one of our everyday cost-saving habits. All official text, including the rulebook, scenarios and card contents, goes through a full translation process and is proofread by experienced native speakers. Please rest assured on that.
notes:
• The publisher’s English vs the Chinese. Their AI versions mostly match, but a few lines differ in meaning:
  • Achilles, psychological illness: the Chinese says Achilles users have a more than 80% higher chance of illness than Theseus users. The publisher’s English says users have “a probability of more than 80%” of falling ill, which is a much stronger claim.
  • Theseus, multiple persons: 我不是数人 means “I am not a multiple person” (that is, not several copies or bodies). The publisher’s English has “I am not counting people at this moment.”
  • Theseus, surgery: 微创面自结构手术 is “micro-incision self-structuring surgery.” The publisher’s English has “minimally invasive facial autostructure surgery”; there is nothing about the face.
  • Memorial tissue: 纪念组织 is “memorial tissue.” The publisher’s English once has “memorial organization,” a mistranslation of 组织 (both “tissue” and “organization”).
  • 浸染, “steeping.” Literally “soaking and dyeing.” 扎染 is the real word for tie-dyeing, so “tie-dyeing” keeps the textile wordplay.
  • 唤醒 “waking,” 调制 “tuning.” 调制 also means “modulation”; the publisher’s English uses “modulated.” I used “tuned” as plainer English.
  • 电子脑, “cyberbrain.” Matches the publisher’s own choice. 原生电子脑 = “native cyberbrain,” 制式电子脑 = “standard cyberbrain.”
  • 意识体, “consciousness.” Literally “consciousness-body,” the stored mind that OPV4 moves around.
  • “Three pieces.” The introduction says three, and the three sections are SOUP, Theseus and Achilles.
  • The image. The diagram credited to “ωistar!α” is probably the same Discord-made OPV diagram shown in the Late Night Wargames interview. Both describe a community member’s picture of OPV levels 1–4 and the two procedures.

relics: Something built, found on the far side of the Moon in the 1940s. Nobody knows who made them. The things carried out of them drive almost everything that follows.
black-box: A Relic product that can be switched on and used, though nobody understands how it works.
opv4: The fourth Obsidian Protocol: the mind runs on a cyberbrain, cut loose from the body it was born in. OPV4 soldiers were first used at scale on Earth in 1990.
soup: Self-Organizing Unstructured Processor: a black liquid found in the Relics. Tuned SOUP is what turns a living brain into a cyberbrain.
cyberbrain: An artificial brain that holds a person's consciousness. It can replace part of the brain or all of it.
theseus: An early cyberbrain procedure that replaces the brain a piece at a time. Gentler, but costly. It went on sale with OPV3 in 1976.
achilles: Dips the whole brain into tuned SOUP at once and comes out with a standard OPV4 cyberbrain. Cheaper and more general than the Theseus Process.

title: Camping Under the Stars
hook: Two brothers lie out under the stars, arguing about a black box. One of them is about to change the world.
html:
The two speakers are Matt and his younger brother, years before “Bucket Town Days.” Matt is the one who loves motorbikes.

“I can’t remember the last time we lay out like this looking at the stars.”

“Yeah… not bad, once in a while!”

“Mm. Once in a while.”

“Hey, I’m telling you, this thing’s a . No doubt about it.”

“Thanks for the tip. And if I remember right, I’m the one who told you that in the first place.”

“So what are you still chewing on? Pick a direction and get going. Aren’t you some hotshot grad from that… what’s-it-called place…?”

“NIT. And that’s exactly where we just got stuck. I already know this can is a pre-tuned set of algorithms. It can’t be unpacked, but it can be used in a program. I just still…”

“So make it into a program! Oh, make a game! Hey, just make a Metal Summons! What number are they up to? I remember when I was a kid I played…”

“Twenty-two… twenty-three never came out before the war started… First, I can’t make Metal Summons, for a lot of reasons I won’t go into. Second, this is a super-coordination algorithm, a seriously powerful one! Putting it in a game would be way too… Okay, I’ll explain one last time. This kind of solution can fold information into a really tiny framework by itself, then optimize the earlier coordination model…”

“Blah blah blah… Can you give me a comparison? Like… it’s fast as a Dukedi? Or it can cheer us up like Nancy does?”

“Stop bringing up Nancy. Okay. You know Ma Whitney’s cowshed? It’s highly automated. There’s a livestock management system in there, something like this, that can look after a lot of cows. Which cow’s calving, how much to feed today, when to slaughter, how to sell for more: that’s the most basic kind of coordination. But what we’ve got here is far more advanced than that. It can handle far more complicated things.”

“Right, right, it’s real clever. So we stick it in a computer and sell it to the hick over the hill?”

“Hick? Oh, you mean the orchard owner?”

“Yeah, him. His son just bought a Landa. Paid 800 for it, the idiot.”

“A Landa?”

“Yeah, a Landa 34. In that state it’s worth 650 tops. Looked like the back axle was about to drop off.”

“Oh.”

“I heard they made some money last year and they’ve been wanting a cowshed like Ma Whitney’s. You tidy this thing up, make it into that whatsit you said…”

“Livestock management system.”

“Right, system! Then I go and fleece him good… and we get ourselves a real Landa, huh? See, I told you! When us two put our heads together, we always come up with something good! Just like last month’s cross-country race…”

“Stop waving food around! Listen. This solution is many, many times more powerful than the system in the Whitney cowshed. I mean more powerful than you can imagine. Using it to run a handful of cows…”

“Even better! We sell it to the cattle ranch in town! That place has as many as thirty cowsheds! The Cavalry tore out their gear a while back. Now it’s all done by hand and they can’t keep up!”

“Oh. So they did tear it out.”

“Yeah, they tore it out. The Cavalry said it was some kind of weak point or whatever. The old man begged them for ages, but in the end they still tore it out. I saw him a few days ago, so tired his eyes couldn’t even move. He’s got to be richer than the hick, right? If this works it won’t just be a Landa. Maybe we could get a Dukedi?! Maybe more, and then we could build a new house! We’d make a goddamn fortune!”

“First, the Ryderson Ranching cattle ranch here is three hundred times the size of Ma Whitney’s shed… Second, never mind a few thousand head. If you really used this, it could raise every cow in the world with room to spare…”

“The whole world! That’s a lot of cows, bro. Did I ever tell you, there’s this video, it says that on pre-war cattle ranches…”

“Yes, I didn’t misspeak! You don’t need to question my sense of numbers! And please don’t tell that dirty joke about the cowgirl! Anyway, it could raise not just every cow in the world today, but pre-war, post-war, future and past ones too. Every cow from the day the goddamn even-toed ungulates first appeared until the Earth is destroyed, it could raise them all at once! And all the whales while it’s at it! Because raising cows is so goddamn easy for it, do you understand? It’s a piece of cake for it! Using it to raise cows is like…”

“Whales aren’t cows, pal. Don’t get so worked up you go stupid!”

If I'm right, this kind of command system will be banned in the future.

“You…”

“Huh? Am I right?”

“…”

“What’s that ‘even-toad ungulants’ thing you just said?”

“I…”

“Okay, okay, no more cow talk. Calm down, huh?”

“…”

“You said before that this thing could be used to… um… lead an army, right?”

“Phew… What I said was, in Dead Man’s Valley out west, the automatic weapons in there are commanded by something similar. Technically, a distributed command system is only similar to this. I reckon ours is a bit more advanced, but I’m not sure. Maybe the military’s solution was made from black boxes too, but it’s hard to know that now.”

“So… how about we sell it to the General? Maybe the Cavalry could use it? Haven’t they always wanted to clear out Dead Man’s Valley?”

“You mean build them a command system too?”

“Yeah? Haven’t they got a few drones and stuff? They’re always in at Old Li’s getting them fixed, creaking away.”

“Hard to say. The General and his crew lived through the . They’ll find it hard to trust this kind of thing again. And if I’m right, this kind of command system will be banned in the future. Maybe it’s already banned and we just don’t know yet. So if we give it to those old fossils, they’ll most likely just mark it up and sell it to the caravan riders.”

“Then let’s just sell it straight to the caravan riders… yawn… I’m sleepy…”

“I don’t know… Actually, back in college, for various reasons I took a minor in sociology. I didn’t take it very seriously, but there was this one little idea that really fascinated me. I even wrote a short paper on it. But the idea didn’t actually work mathematically, so it was only a thought experiment I played with for fun… But this algorithm is so amazing it might make those ideas real.”

“So you hadn’t even worked it out, and you sold our motorbikes, bought this thing, didn’t say a goddamn word to me, and now you’re begging me to help you come up with ideas?”

“One, I’m not begging you for help! Two, I’ve been thinking this whole time, and ever since you got back you’ve been yelling about your motorbikes and distracting me! If you hadn’t kept butting in I’d have worked it out ages ago…”

“Just the motorbikes?! You didn’t just sell the motorbikes! Look! …You burned the goddamn house down too! Didn’t your mom ever tell you not to space out while you’re cooking?! Huh?! Why do you think we’re out here camping? Nostalgia for the Boy Scouts?”

“Oh, here we go again! Sorry! I’m very sorry! But this thing really is more important than any goddamn motorbike. Now be quiet a minute and let me think!”

“And the house! The house!!”

“…”

“…”

“…”

“…”

“Matt?”

“…Hm?”

“Are you asleep?”

“…Pretty much…”

“I’ve got a plan.”

“…yawn… great…”

“Yeah? Do you get what I mean?”

“…Dukedi… 775…”

“No… I’m not talking about a plan to buy a bike…”

“…Whatever… your plan… had better have a house in it…”

“Mm.”

“…Then that’s fine…”

“And not just one or two houses.”

“…Mm…”

“In my plan, there are lots of houses.”

“…Mm…”

“…”

“…”

“As many as the stars.”
notes:
• The two brothers. Matt (马特) is the narrator of “Bucket Town Days.” The brother, never named here, is the one who later built “Big Brain” and the community that became Bucket City. This story shows the night the plan began.
  • NIT. Given as “NIT” in English in the original. The timeline mentions the “Masatuck Institute of Technology” (马萨图克理工大学), so NIT may be a nickname or a different school.
  • 《金属召唤》, Metal Summons. A video game series in the setting, likely a joke on a real shooter franchise. Rendered literally.
  • 统筹, “coordination.” The word means overall planning and allocation of resources. The same word is in the setting’s 统筹核心 (“Coordination Core”), the AI-like black boxes that ran the war armies.
  • 兰达, “Landa.” A motorbike make, by sound.
  • 骑兵队, “the Cavalry.” A local armed group led by “the General” (将军).
  • 莱德森牧业, “Ryderson Ranching.” By sound.
  • The joke. The brother says 偶蹄目 (Artiodactyla, “even-toed ungulates”); Matt mishears it as 呕题目 (roughly “puke topic”). I used “even-toad ungulants” to keep the mishearing.
  • 马帮, “caravan riders.” Literally a horse-caravan gang; the same word comes up in “Bucket Town Days.”
  • Tone. As in the other Matt story, the swearing (他妈) is kept at about the same strength.

black-box: A Relic product that can be switched on and used, though nobody understands how it works.
great-war: The worldwide war that broke out in 2010, fought by automated armies on both sides. A ceasefire on Earth came in 2040.

title: Bucket Town Days
hook: Years later, Matt lays flowers on his brother's grave, in a town that grew into the heart of the League.
html:
Visiting the Grave

The dew was nearly gone. A few chickadees were calling, but with the early morning sun behind them it was hard to tell which branch they were on.

Matt pulled off his gloves and laid a bunch of fresh flowers in front of the headstone.

He looked around. He was the only one in the cemetery.

· · ·

Little brother, you’ve been gone a lot of years now.

Life just keeps getting better.

Bucket Town is Bucket City now, right in the heart of the League. They say our synchronization level here is the highest anywhere. Honestly, I don’t really know what that means, but anyway, it’s a good thing. It means things are going smoothly.

They also say a whole bunch more cities joined the League this year, all hoping to get things going as smoothly as we have, or as Daike Town has.

Nancy passed last year too. A lot of people came to the funeral. I didn’t know any of them, and if you ask me, Nancy didn’t either.

How do I put it?

They all came because they worship you. Loads of them come looking for me, asking if I’ve got any books or notebooks or whatever you left behind. I got sick of it, so I changed my name again and moved a few times, but people still find me.

They say you saved a lot of people. They say you built the best damn community there ever was.

Honestly, all those designs and ideas of yours, I still don’t get them.

When I was young I thought everything was simple. Whatever you said, I understood.

Now I reckon I never understood any of it.

Like, I don’t get why you built a computer that was so goddamn smart, to tell the rest of us what to do, but you wouldn’t listen to it yourself.

It's just, it's a little too good. So good it makes me uneasy.

Sometimes I think it was smarter than you. I remember once I asked you whether Old Li’s crew had time to fix the harvester. You said you didn’t know. I asked Big Brain, and it knew.

So why didn’t you listen to it and get the surgery?

I can’t figure you out.

I came today, but I don’t know when I’ll be back to see you again.

This place is better than it’s ever been, but I can’t seem to stay put.

It’s just, it’s a little too good. So good it makes me uneasy.

I can’t say exactly what it is, but I remember clearly the first time I felt it. It was a few years back, on my seventy-fifth birthday, when Lenny bought me a Dukedi 775.

A Dukedi 775, little brother. A goddamn beauty. I hadn’t laid eyes on one in I don’t know how many years.

After we made our money I collected a dozen or so good bikes. I had several Dukedis, but the 775, the 775 I just could not find. I practically started our Dukedi Club for her alone, just to hear word of one.

I’d given up. Then I asked my daughter-in-law, did Lenny have to run all over the place to find this bike?

Guess what?

She said a few days earlier, when Lenny went to deliver equipment to the factory, Reynard just gave him one.

That’s the factory out in Dead Man’s Valley. They call it Flower Valley now. They say “Dead Man’s Valley” is bad for tourism.

I’d never have thought anyone would come here as a tourist. And you can smell that factory from miles off. Who’d want to go there?

Oh, right, the 775.

It’s not that I wasn’t happy. It just felt like a real coincidence.

A bit too much of a coincidence, and too good. So good it felt wrong.

Like, I think Dukedis are damn great. All the new stuff is pretty good too, really, but it just doesn’t have that Dukedi feel, you know?

But then I see my son likes Dukedis too, and one of my grandson’s buddies has joined our club.

You’d think there’s nothing strange about that. A classic is a classic. It’s no surprise somebody always loves them.

But look. Go to Manka or New Domon and the ads are always for the newest damn bikes. And yet this little quarterback, not even of age, is hanging around with our crowd, saying he fell in love with Dukedis the first time he heard of them.

I asked him, have you ever ridden a Speedflag, a Blue Bolt, a Farani, any of those makes? Don’t young people all like those? He said he feels he has a “connection” with Dukedi. Old Li would call it “fate.” Loads of really good things have come his way through Dukedi, he said, and he’d always liked the look of the bike anyway.

Ah, I can’t explain it.

I think they love the bike the same as I do, but not the same. Like my love is more real.

Maybe I’m just old, and nothing looks right to me anymore.

Anyway, I’m leaving.

When I was young I badly wanted to ride a 775 all the way around the continent.

Back then I didn’t have a 775, and I couldn’t get out of our patch anyway.

A while ago the bridge at Taronia opened. Some caravan rider told me you can ride all the way to Penrose now, and told me to look it up on the terminal myself. I did, and it’s true.

I’d never even thought about where Penrose was.

I hear they don’t allow implants or whatnot there. Doesn’t bother me.

This time I can finally try to ride to the east coast.

Goodbye, old pal.

· · ·

The sun rose slowly. On Highway 85, a brand-new Speedflag headed east.
notes:
• Names. People and places are rendered by sound where no official English exists: 马特 Matt, 南希 Nancy, 莱尼 Lenny, 雷纳德 Reynard, 老李 Old Li, 黛珂镇 Daike Town, 曼卡 Manka, 新多蒙 New Domon, 塔罗尼亚 Taronia, 彭罗斯 Penrose. If the publisher uses different spellings, these should be swapped in.
  • 水桶镇 / 水桶城 is literally “Water-Bucket Town / City”; “Bucket Town” keeps it short.
  • 同盟, “the League.” The card data and the official timeline call this faction 复兴发展同盟, the Reconstruction Development League (RDL); the story uses the short form, so “the League” here. The RDL is run by an AI, “the Guide,” that shapes what people want. That is very likely what Matt is sensing when everything feels “too good” and when the boy’s love of Dukedis seems arranged.
  • Matt’s brother. “Camping Under the Stars” shows the night the brother first plans what became Bucket Town, using a black-box “coordination” algorithm. “Big Brain” is presumably what he built from it.
  • 同步程度, “synchronization level.” Kept literal. Matt doesn’t know what it means, and the story leaves it vague.
  • 大聪明, “Big Brain.” A joking nickname, roughly “Mr. Smarty” or “Big Clever,” for the computer Matt’s brother built.
  • Bike makes. 杜科迪 (Dukedi) sounds like Ducati and is kept as sound. 速旗 (Speedflag, literally “speed banner”), 蓝电 (Blue Bolt, literally “blue electric”) and 法兰尼 (Farani) are rendered by meaning or sound.
  • The ending. The last line has Matt (presumably) riding off on a brand-new Speedflag rather than his Dukedi 775. That’s the original, not a translation slip: it is the same make he asked the boy about, and it seems to be the story’s final hint that his tastes are being nudged too.
  • 缘分, “fate.” A Chinese idea of fated affinity between people or things. “Fate” is the closest short word.
  • Tone. Matt swears a lot (他妈, 他娘的) and talks in rural slang. I kept the swearing at about the same strength and gave him a plain, folksy voice instead of word-for-word phrasing.
quote: Little brother, you've been gone a lot of years now.

title: Late Night Wargames, episode 154
zh: Late Night Wargames 154 采访翻译
hook: Queti's designer sits down with two hosts to tell the story behind the setting: the Moon, its colonies, and the three sides fighting over it.
html:
The source is not a transcript. The interview was in English, with an interpreter. Afterwards the Queti guest (R) wrote this Chinese summary of what was said, with their own comments in brackets. This file translates that summary back into English, so the wording is a paraphrase of a paraphrase, not the exact words said on the show.

relics: Something built, found on the far side of the Moon in the 1940s. Nobody knows who made them. The things carried out of them drive almost everything that follows.
obsidian: The Leighton Group's technology for joining the human mind to machines, released as OPV1 to OPV4. Its long-term aim is to digitize consciousness, which is why many faiths oppose it.
opv4: The fourth Obsidian Protocol: the mind runs on a cyberbrain, cut loose from the body it was born in. OPV4 soldiers were first used at scale on Earth in 1990.
soup: Self-Organizing Unstructured Processor: a black liquid found in the Relics. Tuned SOUP is what turns a living brain into a cyberbrain.
cyberbrain: An artificial brain that holds a person's consciousness. It can replace part of the brain or all of it.
theseus: An early cyberbrain procedure that replaces the brain a piece at a time. Gentler, but costly. It went on sale with OPV3 in 1976.
core: AI-like black boxes from the Relics with immense computing power. The first was found in 1977; they went on to run the automated armies of the Great War.
guide: A Coordination Core put in charge of a whole society: it allocates the resources and steers what people want. Proposed by the scholar Lauren in 2009, it took over the Reconstruction Development League in 2030.
lmc: Set up by the first Space Treaty in 1973 to govern high orbit and the Moon. The A.E. calendar dates from its founding.
hou: The independent state of the Moon and high orbit, declared in 2015. Its basic unit is the company, not the citizen.
gof: A union of farming companies and cooperatives led by Saturn-8, founded in 2031. The media gave them the name for their fight for “free will.”
sleipnir: The city on the Moon that grew up around a giant mass driver in the Rhaetia crater.
